questions.answer:
```cpp
void myHeapSort(std::vector<int>& nums) {
    std::make_heap(nums.begin(), nums.end());                         // O(n): nums becomes a max-heap
    for (auto last = nums.end(); last != nums.begin(); --last)
        std::pop_heap(nums.begin(), last);                            // O(log n): max goes to last-1, heap shrinks by one
}
```

**How it works.** `make_heap(first, last)` rearranges the range into a **max**-heap (default `operator<`): the largest element is at `nums[0]`. `pop_heap(first, last)` swaps the root with the last element of `[first, last)` and then restores the heap property on `[first, last - 1)`; so after the call the maximum sits at position `last - 1`, outside the shrunken heap, in its final place. Calling `pop_heap` with `last` going from `end()` down to `begin() + 1` therefore places the largest, second largest, ... elements from the back: the vector ends up ascending. This is exactly the textbook heapsort (build a max-heap, then repeat deleteMax into the freed slot), done in place.

**Complexity.**
- `make_heap`: **O(n)** (buildHeap; cplusplus.com: up to linear in 3n comparisons).
- Each `pop_heap` on a range of size s: O(log s) <= O(log n); it is called n times: **O(n log n)**. (The last iteration, `last == begin() + 1`, calls `pop_heap` on a 1-element range, which does nothing; you may stop the loop one step earlier.)
- Total O(n) + O(n log n) = **O(n log n)** worst, average and best case. Extra space **O(1)**: everything happens inside `nums`. Not stable (a swap of the root with the last element moves equal keys past each other).

Equivalent library shortcut: `make_heap(...); sort_heap(...);` (`sort_heap` does the same repeated `pop_heap` internally, O(n log n)); the HW asks for the explicit loop.

```cpp
void myHeapSort2(std::vector<int>& nums) {
    std::make_heap(nums.begin(), nums.end());   // O(n)
    std::sort_heap(nums.begin(), nums.end());   // repeated pop_heap internally: O(n log n)
}
```

questions.answer:
```cpp
int closest(const set<int>& s, int x) {            // s must be non-empty; ties go to the smaller value
    auto it = s.lower_bound(x);                      // first element >= x
    if (it == s.end()) return *prev(it);             // every element is < x: the largest one is closest
    if (it == s.begin()) return *it;                 // every element is >= x: the smallest one is closest
    auto before = prev(it);                          // largest element < x
    return (x - *before <= *it - x) ? *before : *it;
}
```

**Cases.** `it = s.lower_bound(x)` is the first element >= x (the successor-or-equal).
- `it == s.end()`: every element is < x, so the closest is the largest element, `*prev(it)` (the last element; the set is non-empty).
- `it == s.begin()`: every element is >= x, so the closest is the smallest, `*it`.
- Otherwise: `*it >= x` is the nearest candidate on the right and `*prev(it) < x` the nearest candidate on the left; compare the two distances (`<=` gives the tie to the smaller value).

**Complexity.** `lower_bound` is a member function: a descent of a balanced BST, O(log n). `prev(it)` is one bidirectional step, O(1); the comparisons and arithmetic are O(1). Total **O(log n)**, space O(1). (Calling the algorithm `std::lower_bound(s.begin(), s.end(), x)` would be O(n) because the iterators of a set cannot jump.) A hash set cannot do this: closest-value queries need order, otherwise O(n) per query.

**For `map<int,string>`:** yes, with `it->first` instead of `*it` (map iterators point to `pair<const int, string>`); `lower_bound` is again a member function with the same O(log n) cost. `map::operator[]` must be avoided on a `const` map and creates entries when used for lookup.

questions.prompt:
**Per-operation complexity of STL calls.** Give the time complexity of each operation. For hash containers give the average case **and** the worst case. n is the number of elements in the container.

1. `unordered_map::find(key)`
2. `unordered_map::operator[](key)` when the key is absent
3. Iterating over all n elements of an `unordered_set`
4. `map::find(key)` and `set::insert(x)`
5. `set::lower_bound(x)` (member function)
6. `std::lower_bound(s.begin(), s.end(), x)` where `s` is a `std::set`
7. `priority_queue::top()`
8. `priority_queue::push(x)` and `priority_queue::pop()`
9. `make_heap(v.begin(), v.end())` on a vector of n elements
10. `vector::push_back(x)` and `vector::insert(v.begin(), x)`
11. `list::insert(pos, x)` / `list::erase(pos)` given an iterator `pos`
12. `std::sort` on a vector of n elements
questions.answer:
| # | Operation | Complexity | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `unordered_map::find` | **O(1) average, O(n) worst** | hash the key, search one bucket; all keys in one bucket gives the worst case |
| 2 | `operator[]`, key absent | **O(1) average, O(n) worst** (plus amortized rehash) | find the bucket, create a default-valued element; may trigger a rehash |
| 3 | iterate all of an `unordered_set` | **O(n)** (with a reasonable load factor) | visits each element once |
| 4 | `map::find`, `set::insert` | **O(log n)** worst case | balanced BST (red-black tree) |
| 5 | `set::lower_bound` (member) | **O(log n)** | one tree descent |
| 6 | `std::lower_bound` on a `set` | **O(n)** | only O(log n) comparisons, but advancing bidirectional iterators takes linear time |
| 7 | `priority_queue::top` | **O(1)** | root of the heap is `front()` of the vector |
| 8 | `priority_queue::push` / `pop` | **O(log n)** each | percolate up / percolate down in a binary heap |
| 9 | `make_heap` | **O(n)** | buildHeap (up to about 3n comparisons) |
| 10 | `push_back` / `insert` at the front | **amortized O(1)** / **O(n)** | occasional reallocation; inserting at the front shifts every element |
| 11 | `list::insert`/`erase` with an iterator | **O(1)** | relink pointers of a doubly linked list |
| 12 | `std::sort` | **O(n log n)** | introsort (quicksort + heapsort fallback), worst case O(n log n) |
rubric: Hash operations (1, 2) given as O(1) average AND O(n) worst case
Ordered container operations and member lower_bound given as O(log n); std::lower_bound on a set recognized as O(n)

questions.prompt:
**Design and analysis: the k largest of n numbers.** You must report the `k` largest of `n` distinct integers (`1 <= k <= n`). Analyze each of these four designs and give a tight time bound in terms of n and k, with the cost of every step justified, plus the extra space:

1. Sort the whole array (`std::sort`) and take the last `k`.
2. Build a max-heap of all n elements (`make_heap`) and call `pop_heap` k times.
3. Keep a **min**-heap of size `k` while scanning the array once.
4. `std::nth_element` (quickselect) to place the k largest at the front.

Then say which one you would use if (i) `k = 10` and `n = 10^8` values arrive as a stream that does not fit in memory, (ii) `k = n/2`, (iii) the data fits in memory, `k` is small, and you need the best worst-case guarantee.
questions.answer:
**1. Sort.** `sort` is O(n log n) in the worst case (introsort); reading the last k is O(k). Total **O(n log n)**, extra space O(1) (in place) - it does far more work than needed because it orders everything.

**2. Build a max-heap and pop k times.** `make_heap` is **O(n)** (buildHeap: the sum of node heights is O(n)). Each `pop_heap` is O(log n) (percolate down in a heap of size <= n); k of them cost k x O(log n). Total **O(n + k log n)**, space O(1) if done in place on the vector. For k <= n / log n this is O(n).

**3. Min-heap of size k.** Each of the n elements is compared with the root in O(1); if it is larger, `pop` + `push` cost O(log k) + O(log k) on a heap of size <= k. Worst case (increasing input) every element enters: **O(n log k)**. Extracting the k results is O(k log k) <= O(n log k). Space **O(k)**, one pass.

**4. nth_element.** Quickselect: **O(n) on average** (cplusplus.com: linear on average), but O(n^2) worst case for the textbook pivot rules (real libraries use introselect, which falls back to a heap-based selection and so cannot exceed O(n log n)). The k largest end up in the front (unordered); sorting just those costs another O(k log k). Space O(1).

**Choices.**
- (i) **Design 3**: one pass, O(k) = 10 elements of memory, works on a stream; the cost per element is a comparison with the root (and only rarely a log k = log 10 push/pop). Designs 1, 2 and 4 need all n values in memory.
- (ii) k = n/2: design 1 O(n log n); design 2 O(n + (n/2) log n) = O(n log n); design 3 O(n log(n/2)) = O(n log n); design 4 O(n) average. **Quickselect (4)** is asymptotically best (plus an O(k log k) = O(n log n) sort only if the output must be ordered).
- (iii) Small k, memory is fine, and a worst-case guarantee is required: **design 2** has a deterministic O(n + k log n), which is O(n) for small k, with no bad-pivot risk. Design 3 is O(n log k) worst case which is also near-linear for small k but not tight with O(n); design 4 is O(n) only on average (O(n^2) worst for the textbook version).

questions.answer:
```cpp
vector<string> misspelled(const vector<string>& dictionary, const vector<string>& document) {
    unordered_set<string> dict(dictionary.begin(), dictionary.end());   // D inserts: O(D) average
    set<string> bad;                                         // distinct misspellings, kept sorted
    for (const string& w : document)                         // n lookups: O(n) average
        if (dict.count(w) == 0)
            bad.insert(w);                                   // O(log m) each
    return vector<string>(bad.begin(), bad.end());           // already in sorted order: O(m)
}
```

**Container choices.**
- **Dictionary: `unordered_set<string>`.** We only ask "is this word present?" many times; a hash set answers it in O(1) average and its order is irrelevant.
- **Result: `set<string>`.** We need the distinct misspellings *in sorted order*. A `set` removes duplicates on insert and iterates in sorted order, so no separate sort is needed. (Alternative: collect them in an `unordered_set` and `sort` a vector at the end - same bound O(m log m).)

**Complexity (strings as O(1)).**
- Build the dictionary: D inserts x O(1) average = **O(D)**.
- Scan the document: n lookups x O(1) average = **O(n)**.
- Each misspelled occurrence calls `bad.insert`, O(log m) in a set of at most m elements; there are at most n of them: **O(n log m)** worst case if every word of the document is misspelled (n occurrences), and in general O(n_bad log m). Copying out `bad` into the vector: O(m).
- Total **O(D + n + n log m)**, i.e. O(D + n log m) because m <= n, average case (the hash part is average case; the set part is worst case).

With words of length up to L: hashing and each equality check cost O(L), each tree comparison costs O(L): O(DL + nL + n L log m) = **O(DL + nL log m)**.

**Why not put everything in `set<string>`?** The dictionary lookups would cost O(log D) each: O(n log D) instead of O(n) - the hash set is faster for pure membership.
rubric: Dictionary stored in an unordered_set<string> (membership only)
